blocks.text: Ever wondered how to retrieve data from multiple tables in a database efficiently? Discover the power of SQL joins and subqueries to unlock complex data relationships.

blocks.markdown: In SQL, retrieving data from multiple tables is a common task, often requiring the use of joins and subqueries. Joins allow you to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them. Subqueries, on the other hand, are queries nested inside another query, providing a way to perform operations that depend on the results of another query.

blocks.title: Join
blocks.text: A join is an SQL operation that combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them.

blocks.markdown: There are several types of joins in SQL, including INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and FULL JOIN. Each type serves a different purpose and can be used depending on the desired result.

rows: Returns rows when there is a match in both tables.
Returns all rows from the left table, and the matched rows from the right table.
Returns all rows from the right table, and the matched rows from the left table.
Returns rows when there is a match in one of the tables.

blocks.title: Using INNER JOIN
blocks.prompt: Write an SQL query to retrieve the names of all students and their corresponding course titles from the 'students' and 'courses' tables.

steps.text: Identify the common column between the two tables, which is 'course_id'.
Use INNER JOIN to combine the tables based on 'course_id'.
steps.latex: SELECT students.name, courses.title FROM students INNER JOIN courses ON students.course_id = courses.id;

blocks.answer: SELECT students.name, courses.title FROM students INNER JOIN courses ON students.course_id = courses.id;

blocks.markdown: Subqueries can be categorized into two types: correlated and uncorrelated. An uncorrelated subquery is independent of the outer query, while a correlated subquery depends on the outer query for its values.

blocks.title: Correlated Subquery
blocks.text: A subquery that uses values from the outer query, making it dependent on the outer query for execution.

blocks.title: Correlated Subquery Example
blocks.prompt: Find the names of students who have enrolled in more than 3 courses using a correlated subquery.

steps.text: Use a correlated subquery to count the number of courses per student.
Filter students with more than 3 courses.
steps.latex: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE enrollments.student_id = students.id) > 3;

blocks.answer: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE enrollments.student_id = students.id) > 3;

blocks.title: Key Point
blocks.text: A correlated subquery is evaluated once for each row processed by the outer query, whereas an uncorrelated subquery is evaluated once for the entire query.

blocks.markdown: In some cases, subqueries can be rewritten as joins, which can improve query performance. This is particularly useful when the subquery is uncorrelated.

points: Joins combine rows from multiple tables based on a related column.
Subqueries can be correlated or uncorrelated, with different dependencies on the outer query.
Rewriting subqueries as joins can enhance performance.
